tabs.quote:
B0062 · Indicators of Global Climate Change 2022: annual update of large-scale indicators of the state of the climate system and human influence
The purpose of this effort, grounded in an open data, open science approach, is to make annually updated reliable global climate indicators available in the public domain (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8000192, Smith et al., 2023a).

B0102 · 1 Introduction
An important purpose of the exercise is to make these indicators widely available and understood. Plans for a web dashboard are discussed in Sect. 10 and code and data availability in Sect. 11, and conclusions are presented in Sect. 12. Data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8000192 (Smith et al., 2023a).

B0530 · 11 Code and data availability
The carbon budget calculation is available from https://github.com/Rlamboll/AR6CarbonBudgetCalc (Lamboll and Rogelj, 2023). The code and data used to produce other indicators are available in repositories under https://github.com/ClimateIndicator (Smith et al., 2023b). All data are available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8000192 (Smith et al., 2023a). Data are provided under the CC-BY 4.0 Licence.

B0813 · References
Smith, C., Walsh, T., Forster, P. M., Gillett, N., Hauser, M., Lamb, W., Lamboll, R., Palmer, M., Ribes, A., Schumacher, D., Seneviratne, S., Trewin, B., and von Schuckmann, K.: Indicators of Global Climate Change 2022 (v2023.06.02), Zenodo [data set], https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8000192, 2023a.

B0107 · 2.1 Datasets
The IGCC GMT is an average of four sources: Had CRUT5, NOAAGlobalTemp, Berkeley Earth and Kadow et al.

B0267 · 4 Relationship between anthropogenic emissions and global warming
Lower and Upper here are 95\(\%\) confidence lower and upper limits. The GMT increase is the mean of the four temperature datasets. The 7-point smoothing is the result of 7-yr running mean time series

B0252 · 4 Relationship between anthropogenic emissions and global warming
Each 1000 Gt C of cumulative \(CO_{2}\) emissions is assessed to likely cause a 0.49 \(\degree\)C increase in GMT with a range [0.25–0.74]\(\degree\)C for the raw time series or a 0.51 \(\degree\)C with a range [0.34–0.68]\(\degree\)C for the 7-yr running mean time series (Table 1), slightly higher than a 0.45 \(\degree\)C with a range [0.27–0.63]\(\degree\)C of the IPCC AR6 (IPCC 2021).

B0255 · 4 Relationship between anthropogenic emissions and global warming
For instance, each 1000 Gt C of cumulative \(CO_{2}\) emissions is assessed to likely cause 0.51 \(\degree\)C and 0.51 \(\degree\)C increases in GMT with ranges [0.33–0.69]\(\degree\)C and [0.35–0.67]\(\degree\)C for the 5-yr and 9-yr running mean time series, respectively.

B0298 · 5 The CCM and theoretical foundation for the CPA of one country under equal EHRs
The simulated GMT of the CCM well demonstrates the historical growth changes of the observed GMT (Fig. 4b), also reflecting that the long-term warming changes in the GMT are the result of cumulative human emissions. In 2021–2023, the observed GMTs relative to 1850–1900 were \([1.03–1.22]^{\circ}C\) , \([1.06–1.26]^{\circ}C\) , and \([1.35–1.55]^{\circ}C\) , respectively, with the simulated values corresponding to \(1.19^{\circ}C\) , \(1.21^{\circ}C\) , and \(1.23^{\circ}C\), respectively. The significant interannual variability of the 2023 El Niño event contributes significantly to the observed increase in the GMT in 2023 (Raghuraman et al. 2024).

B0328 · 6.1 Basic metrics
The EPC clearly eliminates intergenerational and regional differences. In theory, it does not change with time and region. This is the objective basis for CPA within one country or region (national CPA for short) under equal EHRs. According to the results mentioned above, if set \(T = 2^{\circ}C\) , the corresponding global cumulative \(CO_{2}\) emissions \(C_{TW}\)will be 4000 Gt C, respectively (Table 1).
